title: Malolactic conversion
what: A second, bacterial fermentation after the alcoholic one. You can block it with SO₂, inoculate a selected strain, or let it start on its own.

steps: The bacteria also break down citric acid
making diacetyl, which peaks as the malic acid runs out
so the wine can smell of butter and cream
A wine bottled with malic acid and live bacteria
so a blocked wine needs SO₂ and sterile filtration; a converted one is more stable

choose: Convert Côte d'Or reds: village and Premier Cru rules allow at most 0.4 g/L malic acid at bottling. Block it for crisp Mosel Riesling, whose acidity is the point. Inoculation is faster and surer.
exam: A classic question: why does a producer choose, or avoid, malolactic conversion? Give acidity, buttery notes and stability, and name a wine for each choice.

check.question: An off-dry Mosel Riesling with 6 g/L malic acid is heading for bottle. Why does the cellar master block MLF and sterile-filter?
options: To keep its sharp acidity and stop the conversion starting in bottle
Because the bacteria would eat the residual sugar and make it dry
check.answer: To keep its sharp acidity and stop the conversion starting in bottle
check.why: Much of Riesling's bright acidity is malic, and it balances the sugar. Without SO₂ and sterile filtration, bacteria could convert it in the bottle; its residual sugar needs sterile filtration anyway.

sources: law.md#Rules that bite in the simulation
simplification: Game simplification: a spontaneous conversion gives more diacetyl than an inoculated one (in reality strain, oxygen, citric acid and SO₂ decide), and conversion in bottle is not modelled.
